9.1.summary:
Wrongdoing isn't just a private failing; it's a kind of offence against the order of the universe itself. Nature made people to help one another, so injustice goes against what we were made for. Lying does too, because nature is bound up with truth, and careless untruth means you've let your sense of what's real go slack.

Marcus adds that treating pleasure as good and pain as bad is also a kind of impiety. If you think that way, you end up resenting the world whenever the wrong people prosper, fearing what's coming, and bending the rules to get what you want. Nature hands out pleasure and pain, life and death, praise and disgrace without favouritism, and the wise response is to be just as even-handed about them.
9.1.today: Think of how quickly a good week turns sour when a less careful colleague gets the promotion, or how often a small lie starts as "just smoothing things over". Marcus would say both come from the same place: deciding that comfort and getting your way are what really count.

9.2.summary:
The best life would be one that ends without ever having tasted lying, pretence, self-indulgence or arrogance. The next best is to leave once you've had your fill of them. Then Marcus turns on himself: has experience still not taught you to get away from all that?

He compares a corrupted mind to a plague. A disease in the air harms us as bodies, like any animal, but a rotten character harms us in what makes us human, which is far worse.

9.3.summary:
Death is one of nature's ordinary processes, like growing up, going grey or giving birth, and the sensible attitude is neither to dismiss it nor rush towards it, but to wait for it calmly. Marcus compares it to waiting for a baby to arrive: something natural that comes in its own time.

He then offers a more down-to-earth comfort. Look at what you'll be leaving behind, including people who don't share your values. You should still care for them and bear with them gently. But the one thing that might make you cling to life, living among like-minded people, isn't on offer, and the friction of living with others can make you almost glad to go before you lose yourself too.
9.3.today: Most of us spend more energy avoiding the thought of death than waiting for it calmly. Marcus's half-wry comfort is familiar to anyone who has sat through a bitter family argument or a toxic office and thought, wearily, that there are worse things than not having to do this forever.

9.4.summary: When you do wrong, the person you damage most is yourself. Others may lose something external, but you lose something worse: you make yourself into a worse person. For a Stoic, your character is the only thing that's truly yours to ruin.

9.5.summary: You can do wrong by failing to act, not only by acting. Standing by when you could help, or keeping quiet when you should speak, can be just as unjust as doing harm directly.
9.5.today: Watching a colleague get blamed for your mistake and saying nothing, or seeing someone struggle with a pram on the stairs and looking at your phone instead, are both ways of doing wrong without lifting a finger.

9.6.summary: Three things in the present moment are all you need: seeing things clearly and judging them well, acting for the good of others, and accepting whatever happens. None of these depends on the past or the future, and together they're enough for a good life.

9.7.summary: A four-part instruction to himself: clear away runaway imaginings, rein in wants, put out cravings, and keep your judgement in charge of itself. The aim is a mind that's steered by reason, not dragged about by whatever picture or urge turns up.
9.7.today: Think of lying awake rehearsing an argument that never happens, or opening the fridge or the shopping app for no real reason. The habit is noticing the pull and deciding for yourself, not letting the pull decide.

9.8.summary: All living creatures share one life, and all reasoning beings share one mind, in the same way that we all walk on one earth, see by one light and breathe one air. Marcus is reminding himself that your power to think isn't a private possession; it's a share in something you hold in common with every other person.

9.9.summary:
Like is drawn to like throughout nature. Earth settles with earth, water runs together, fire leaps to join fire. Among living things the pull gets stronger: bees swarm, cattle herd, birds raise their young together. Among people it becomes friendships, families, communities, even treaties in war. Higher still, the stars are linked though far apart.

Yet people, who should feel this pull most, are the ones who forget it and try to go it alone. Marcus says they can't really manage it. Our social nature is too strong, and you're more likely to find a lump of earth touching nothing earthy than a person cut off completely from others.
9.9.today: Even the person who insists they don't need anyone still reads the reviews, joins the forum about their hobby, waves at the neighbour, or wants someone to tell about their day. Notice how much of your life, even on a quiet day, is quietly woven into other people's.

9.10.summary: Fruit isn't only something vines produce. People, the gods and the universe all bear fruit in their proper season. So does reason: it yields good for everyone and for itself, and what it produces is more reason, good thinking passed on to others.

9.11.summary: If someone is doing wrong, try to show them a better way. If you can't, that's exactly what your patience is for. The gods themselves are patient with such people and even help them get the health, money and reputation they want. If the gods can be that generous, nothing stops you from being kind as well.
9.11.today: The relative who keeps sharing misleading posts, or the teenager who won't listen: explain once, calmly, if you can. If it doesn't land, patience isn't giving up. It's the other tool you've been given.

9.12.summary: Work neither like someone hard done by nor like someone after sympathy or applause. Want only one thing: to act, or hold back, as the good of others requires.
9.12.today: It's the difference between sighing loudly so everyone knows how much you're doing, and posting about your long hours hoping for admiration, versus simply getting on with what needs doing and stopping when it's done.

9.13.summary: Today Marcus says he has escaped all his troubles, then corrects himself: he has thrown them out. They were never outside him but in his own opinions about things. Change the judgement and the trouble goes with it.
9.13.today: The traffic jam, the unanswered email, the dismissive remark in a meeting: the irritation that follows you home is mostly the story you're telling about them, and that story is the part you can put down.

9.14.summary: Everything is the same old story: familiar from experience, over quickly, and made of nothing precious. Life now is just as it was for the people we've already buried. Marcus is deflating the sense that the present is uniquely important.

9.15.summary: Things and events just sit there. They don't know anything about themselves and don't pass any verdict. The judging is done by your own mind, which means the verdict, and how you feel about it, is your responsibility.

9.16.summary: What makes a reasoning, social person good or bad lies in what they do, not in what happens to them. Your virtue and your failings are in your actions and choices, never in what you passively suffer.

9.17.summary: A stone thrown into the air isn't harmed by coming down, nor helped by having gone up. Rising and falling, gaining and losing, are just what happens to things. Marcus is hinting that our own ups and downs, success and decline, are no different.

9.18.summary: Look closely at what really drives the people whose opinions you fear. You'll see what sort of judges they are, and how poorly they judge even themselves. Their verdict on you will start to seem far less worth worrying about.
9.18.today: The people whose comments you dread online, or whose approval you chase at work, are often just as muddled and anxious as anyone. Seeing that clearly takes the sting out of their judgement.

9.19.summary: Everything is changing, including you. In a sense you're constantly being undone and remade, and so is the whole universe. Marcus is reminding himself that change and loss aren't interruptions to life; they're what life is made of.

9.20.summary: Someone else's wrongdoing is theirs. Leave it with them instead of picking it up and carrying it around as your own grievance.
9.20.today: When a driver cuts you up or a friend lets you down, you can choose not to retell it all day. The wrong was done once; you don't have to keep doing it to yourself.

9.21.summary:
Endings aren't evil. Your childhood ended, then your youth, then your prime, and each change was a small death. Marcus also looks back at the different stages of his own upbringing, each household and period of life giving way to the next. None of those endings was anything to fear.

So why fear the last change, the ending of life itself? It's the same kind of thing, just on a larger scale.
9.21.today: Think of leaving school, moving out of a childhood home, or a job you once couldn't imagine leaving. Each felt like an ending, and in a way it was, yet you came through it as part of the ordinary flow of a life.

9.22.summary: Check three minds without delay. Your own, to make sure it's fair. The mind of the universe, to remember what you're part of. And your neighbour's, to work out whether they acted out of ignorance or knew what they were doing, and to remember that their mind is related to yours.
9.22.today: Before firing off a sharp reply to a colleague, ask whether your own reaction is fair, remember the bigger picture, and consider whether they simply didn't know something you do.

9.23.summary: You're one part of a society, so each thing you do should play its part in that shared life. Any action with no connection, near or far, to the common good pulls your life apart and stops it being whole. Marcus likens it to rebellion, like one person in a public assembly breaking away from what everyone has agreed.

9.24.summary: Human affairs are like children squabbling and playing, or like little souls hauling corpses about. Marcus is borrowing an image from Epictetus of a person as a small soul carrying a dead body. Seen that way, the gloomy pictures of the underworld seem almost more true to life than our self-important bustle.

9.25.summary: A method of looking at things: separate what something essentially is from the stuff it's made of, study that, then ask how long a thing of its kind can last at most. It's a way of cutting through appearances and seeing both what a thing really is and how temporary it is.

9.26.summary: You've put yourself through endless trouble by not being content to let your mind simply do its proper job. Marcus is telling himself that the problems came from wanting more than reason could give, and then he cuts himself off: enough of that.

9.27.summary:
When someone criticises you, hates you or spreads something hurtful, look closely at the kind of person they are. You'll find there's no need to worry about what they think of you.

But that isn't permission to look down on them. You should still wish them well, because by nature they're your friends. Even the gods help such people get the things they care about.
9.27.today: When a stranger leaves a nasty comment or a former friend talks behind your back, picture what's going on in their life and head. You'll usually find their opinion is no reason to lose sleep, and it's still possible to wish them well.

9.28.summary:
The world goes round in the same cycles, age after age. Either a divine mind acts on each event, in which case accept what it does, or it set things going once and the rest follows, or it's all just atoms. Put simply: if there's a god, all is well; if it's all chance, you at least don't have to act at random.

Soon the earth will cover us all, then change itself, and keep changing forever. Watching wave after wave of change, and how fast it comes, you'll stop putting much value on anything that doesn't last.

9.29.summary:
The universe sweeps everything along like a flooded river. Marcus is scornful of politicians who think they're doing philosophy. His own advice is to do what's needed now, without looking round for an audience, and without waiting for a perfect society like the one in Plato's Republic. Be glad if even a small thing goes well.

You can't force people to change their minds, and without that you only get grudging obedience. Alexander the Great, his father Philip and the Athenian statesman Demetrius of Phalerum must answer for whether they truly served the common good. If they were just playing the hero, Marcus doesn't have to copy them. Philosophy's work is simple and modest.
9.29.today: Think of wanting to fix your whole workplace, family or town at once and feeling defeated when it doesn't happen. A better aim is to do the next useful thing well, without posting about it, and count a small improvement as a real win.

9.30.summary:
Picture humanity from high above: countless crowds, ceremonies, voyages in storm and calm, people being born, living together and dying. Add all who lived long ago, all who will come after you, and whole nations who've never heard of you.

Many don't know your name, many will soon forget it, and those praising you now may soon be finding fault. Fame after death, reputation, all of it, is worth nothing. Marcus means this literally, and he's saying it to himself as emperor.
9.30.today: A viral post is forgotten in days, and a career milestone that felt huge is a line on a CV a few years later. Seen from far enough away, the follower count or the colleague's praise shrinks to its real size.

9.31.summary: Two rules for two kinds of thing. What happens to you from outside, meet without being thrown. What comes from inside, your own choices, make just, which means actions aimed at the good of others, because that's what you're made for.

9.32.summary: Much of what bothers you exists only in your own opinion, and you can clear it away. That frees up room to think on a bigger scale: the whole universe, the endless stretch of time, how quickly each thing changes, how short the time is between birth and death, and how vast the stretches before and after. Against that backdrop, most worries lose their grip.
9.32.today: The awkward thing you said at a party, or the slight in a group chat, feels huge at two in the morning. Thinking for a moment about the age of the stars or how many people have lived before you can give the worry its proper, tiny size.

9.33.summary: Everything you see will soon decay, and the people who watch it decay will soon follow. Someone who dies very old ends up in the same state as someone who dies young. Marcus states this plainly, as a fact to steady himself, not to frighten.

9.34.summary: Ask what really guides the people whose opinions you worry about, what they spend their time on, and why they love and admire what they do. Imagine their souls laid bare. The idea that their blame could hurt you or their praise could help you starts to look absurd.
9.34.today: Think of the people whose likes, comments or performance reviews you anxiously track. Picture what actually drives them day to day, and their thumbs-up or frown becomes less of a verdict on your worth.

9.35.summary: Losing something is just a change, and change is how nature works. Through it everything happens as it should, as it always has and always will. Would you really claim that the world has always been bad, and that none of the gods has ever been able to put it right, so it's stuck forever in misery? Marcus finds that far less believable than accepting change as good.

9.36.summary: Look at what everything is made of and it's rather unglamorous: water, dust, bones, muck. Marble is the earth's hardened skin, gold and silver are its deposits, fine clothes are just hair, and the prized purple dye comes from shellfish blood. Even the breath of life is just another substance, always shifting. Marcus is stripping the lustre off things people prize.
9.36.today: Strip a designer label, a new car or the latest phone down to plastic, metal and fabric, and the hold it has on you loosens a little. Marcus's purple dye is today's luxury logo.

9.37.summary: Marcus snaps at himself: enough of this miserable life, the grumbling and the playacting. What's bothering you? Nothing here is new. Look at the thing itself, at what it is and what it's made of; there's nothing else to it. Now become simpler and better towards the gods. Whether you study these things for a hundred years or three, the lesson is the same.

9.38.summary: If someone has done wrong, the harm falls on them, not you. And perhaps they haven't done wrong at all. Two quick checks before you get upset: whose problem is it, and are you even sure it happened?
9.38.today: The friend who didn't reply to your message may be ill or busy, not snubbing you. And if they really are being rude, that's a mark on their character, not yours.

9.39.summary: Either the universe comes from a single intelligent source and works like one body, in which case a part shouldn't complain about what's done for the good of the whole, or it's just atoms mixing and scattering. Either way, why be upset? Ask your own mind: are you dead, corrupted, faking, turned into an animal, just following the herd? If not, you're fine.

9.40.summary:
Change what you pray for. Instead of asking the gods to make things happen or not happen, ask for freedom from the fear, craving or distress itself. If the gods can help at all, they can help with that. And even if these things are in your own power, it's better to use that power freely than to grovel for what isn't.

Marcus gives examples: one person prays to sleep with a certain woman, you pray not to want to; another prays to be rid of a burden, you pray not to long for release; another prays not to lose a child, you pray not to be afraid of losing him. The last one is hard, and he doesn't soften it.
9.40.today: Instead of hoping the interview goes well, you could hope to stay calm whichever way it goes. Instead of wishing your ex would text, you might wish to stop checking. Even worry about a sick child can be held as a wish for courage, not only for a result.

9.41.summary:
Marcus quotes Epicurus, founder of a rival school, who said that when he was ill he didn't talk about his symptoms but kept discussing philosophy, keeping his mind calm while his body suffered, and wouldn't let the doctors make a grand drama of it.

Do the same, in sickness or anything else. Every philosophical school agrees on this much: never give up thinking clearly whatever happens, don't get dragged into idle chat with people who don't understand, and keep your attention on what you're doing now and the mind you're doing it with.
9.41.today: Being ill or stressed tends to shrink every conversation down to the problem. Marcus suggests you can still talk about books, ideas or other people's lives, and not let the illness, the deadline or the doctor's grave face take over everything.

9.42.summary:
When someone's behaviour outrages you, ask whether a world without such people is possible. It isn't, so don't demand the impossible. Remembering this makes you gentler towards each one. Nature also gives you a counter to every fault, such as gentleness for the fool, and you can always try to set someone straight. Besides, they haven't harmed your mind, which is the only place real harm can happen.

And look at yourself. If you're shocked when an untaught person acts badly, you should have expected it. If you call someone ungrateful, ask why you trusted them or why you wanted repayment. Kindness is its own reward, just as the eye wants no payment for seeing.
9.42.today: When a flatmate leaves the dishes again or someone you helped never says thank you, it helps to admit you knew this might happen. If you did the favour hoping to be repaid, the disappointment is partly your own doing, and the good of having helped is already yours.
